intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

paragraphs.text: CMS11 is a congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by defects in rapsyn, a 43-kD postsynaptic protein that is essential for clustering of the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the motor endplate. The endplates show decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR and impaired postsynaptic morphologic development (Ohno et al., 2002). Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients present in the first year of life and a few present later. Nearly one-third have arthrogryposis or other congenital malformations at birth, and intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises. Most patients respond well to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations. The malformations included an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was restricted predominantly to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and the patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors. Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor were absent. Repetitive stimulation at 3 Hz produced a decremental response, but a single nerve stimulus did not evoke a repetitive compound muscle action potential. The authors considered this a newly recognized form of congenital myasthenia with distinctive ethnic clustering.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency who had a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity at birth. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue, he spent a total of 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, metabolic testing, and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. A muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) studied 4 patients with endplate AChR deficiency who had no mutations in the AChR subunit genes and identified 3 recessive mutations in the RAPSN gene. One patient was compound heterozygous for L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3, 2 patients were homozygous for N88K, and 1 patient carried N88K and a 553ins5 mutation that causes a frameshift in TPR5. Expression studies in HEK cells showed that none of the mutations hindered rapsyn self-association, but all 3 diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified 2 mutations in E-box sequences in the RAPSN promoter region in 8 patients with CMS. Patient 1 carried a -27C-G mutation, and the allele harboring this mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Patients 2 through 8 were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations, and they carried a -38A-G mutation. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays and luciferase reporter assays showed that both mutations altered binding of nuclear factors and impaired transcriptional activity.
